blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
This is our twenty-second show together!
Today we climb the tallest mountain on Earth with a man who cannot see it, and we dive under the sea to meet an animal with three hearts!
One story is about courage.
One story is about a body full of surprises.
Let's go!
Erik Weihenmayer was born with weak eyes, and his eyesight faded slowly until, as a young boy, he could not see at all.
But losing his sight did not stop him.
He learned to climb rocks by touch, feeling every crack with his fingers, and listening to the voices of his friends.
Step by step, his courage grew.
He wore thick garments against the cold wind, and he kept going even when his hands got small wounds from ice and stone.
Then came his greatest climb: Mount Everest, the tallest mountain in the world.
Guided by his friends' voices and bells, Erik reached the top — the first blind person ever to do it, to the delight of his whole team, who erupted with cheers.
He did not stop there.
He went on to climb the highest peak on every continent, seven mountains in all.
Touch was his primary guide, and courage was his engine.
Erik says what is inside you is stronger than what stands in your way.
Now dive with me into the sea and meet the octopus, a soft animal with no bones at all.
It has not one heart, but three!
Two small hearts, called branchial hearts, push blood to its gills, where the blood picks up oxygen from the water.
Then a third, bigger heart, the systemic heart, sends the oxygen-rich blood around the body, to every cell.
And here is the strangest part: the octopus's blood is blue!
Our blood is red because it uses iron, but octopus blood uses copper, and copper turns it blue.
When the octopus swims fast, its big heart stops for a while.
Do not worry — the octopus is not dead.
It just gets too tired to keep pumping.
That is why octopuses usually crawl along the sea floor instead of swimming.
It is no coincidence that they are such good crawlers: eight soft arms, covered in suckers, can grip rocks and squeeze the whole body through tiny gaps.
One octopus slipped out of its pen in an aquarium and escaped back to the sea!
With three hearts, blue blood, and a body of soft flesh, the octopus is alive with surprises.
Here's today's idiom: "pull someone's leg." It does not mean you really pull a leg!
It means you tease someone with a joke.
Listen to this: Tom told his friend Sam that a shark lived in the school swimming pool.
Sam put on his swimming hat and ran to look.
Then Tom laughed and said, "I was only pulling your leg!" When someone pulls your leg, they are joking, not telling the truth.
Let's think about our stories.
A blind climber reached the top of the world, and an octopus carries three hearts in its soft body.
Two questions for you.
First: Erik climbed by touch and by listening.
If you could not see, what would help you most — touch, sound, or smell?
Second: if you had three hearts like an octopus, what would you do with the extra one?
Talk about it with your father and mother!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Remember: courage can carry you up any mountain, and a joke is only fun when everyone laughs.
Stay curious!
See you tomorrow morning!
